## Research Report: Does Opening a Bedroom Window or Door Improve Sleep Quality?

**Conclusion: The claim is largely supported, with an important nuance — opening a window appears more effective than opening a door alone.**

Multiple peer-reviewed studies support the idea that improving bedroom ventilation by opening a window improves sleep quality. The primary mechanism is the reduction of indoor carbon dioxide (CO₂) levels, which accumulate overnight in closed bedrooms and are associated with poorer sleep.

**Key evidence:**

- A **field intervention study** conducted by the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) involving 40 bedrooms found that opening a window or door significantly reduced bedroom CO₂ concentrations during sleep. However, **subjective and objective sleep quality and next-day cognitive performance improved only when the window was open** — not when only the door was opened. This suggests that a door alone may not provide sufficient airflow to meaningfully improve sleep. ([DTU Orbit](https://orbit.dtu.dk/en/publications/the-effects-of-bedroom-windowdoor-opening-on-bedroom-air-quality-/))

- An earlier study of 17 healthy volunteers similarly found that window/door opening reduced CO₂ levels and improved sleep, with **87% of participants reporting sound sleep with the window open versus 70% with it closed**. ([Wiley/Indoor Air](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/ina.12435))

- Chamber studies showed that when CO₂ rose from ~800 ppm to ~1,700 ppm (i.e., worse ventilation), **sleep onset latency increased**, indicating reduced sleep quality. Keeping CO₂ below ~750 ppm meant air quality was good enough not to affect sleep. ([DTU News](https://www.dtu.dk/english/newsarchive/2023/05/ventilate-your-bedroom-at-night-you-perform-better-the-next-day))

- An international study as part of an ASHRAE project confirmed that currently prescribed minimum ventilation rates for bedrooms may be **too low**, resulting in disturbed sleep. ([Waseda University](https://www.waseda.jp/top/en/news/86065))

**Bottom line:** Your conviction is well-founded. Opening a bedroom window improves ventilation, lowers CO₂, and is linked to better sleep quality and next-day performance. Opening just the door helps somewhat but appears less effective than a window.
